title: Four Minutes of Darkness at Noon
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I'd dismissed the fuss around eclipse tourism for years, mildly baffled by people who'd fly across continents to watch the sun vanish for four minutes.
Narrator: Having now stood beneath totality myself, I owe every one of those people an unreserved apology, because nothing I'd read prepared me for what actually happened.
Narrator: [carefully] The temperature dropped noticeably in the final minutes before totality, and birds that had been singing all morning fell into an unsettling, collective silence.
Narrator: Then the sun simply disappeared, not dimmed, not clouded over, but replaced entirely by a black disc ringed with pale, trembling light.

Narrator: [reflective] Around me, strangers who'd been chatting idly moments earlier went completely quiet, as though something had reached into the crowd and switched off our capacity for small talk.
Narrator: I'd expected to feel awe, and I did, but what surprised me was an accompanying sense of scale I hadn't braced myself for at all.

Narrator: [honestly] For four minutes, I was watching, with my own unaided eyes, celestial bodies larger and farther away than my mind could genuinely process, aligned with a precision no human hand arranged.
Narrator: A thought returned to me, of the sun and moon each running their course, calculated with such exactness that eclipses can be predicted centuries in advance.
Narrator: [gently] Standing there, that precision stopped being an abstract fact I'd nodded along to and became something I felt directly, almost physically, in my chest.
Narrator: When totality ended and the first blinding sliver of sun reappeared, several people around me were openly crying, and I understood exactly why, without needing it explained.
Narrator: [calmly] I've since stopped being baffled by the people who travel across continents for four minutes of darkness in daylight.
Narrator: I'm already quietly calculating whether I could reach the next path of totality, wherever on earth that turns out to be.
